newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain strike turnout disputed by government, unions.
newsitem.headline: Spain strike turnout disputed by government, unions.

text.p: Spain's conservative government said only 15 percent of civil servants heeded a call for a walkout on Wednesday in protest against a wage freeze aimed at helping the country qualify for a European single currency.

However unions, who called two million civil servants to stop work for 24 hours in protest against a freeze on their 1997 salaries, estimated 81 percent had stayed away. It was the first such stoppage since the government took office.
"From early estimates we can say that around 15 percent of civil servants called to strike have gone out," chief government spokesman Miguel Angel Rodriguez told local television.
If accurate, the government's figures would make the stoppage one of the least successful in recent years.
The General Workers' Union (UGT), one of the top labour groups, estimated the proportion of strikers rose to 89.5 percent in Madrid and 85 percent in Barcelona.

Union leaders said workers also took to the streets in regional capitals to protest against the wage freeze which the government says is vital to meet its single-currency goals. More demonstrations were planned throughout the day.
Trade unions warned on Tuesday the strike would strip hospitals, schools, postal services, courts, public television stations and airports of a large percentage of their staff.
But Rodriguez said on average, only 40 percent of post office workers had gone on strike, while in education the figure fell to 24 percent. Only four percent of airport workers stayed away, he said.
Buses and other transport services, organised under a different trade union, were largely unaffected.
"There is absolute normality. Transport, schools, hospitals and public services are all working," Rodriguez said.
However, Madrid's Barajas airport was forced to cancel a number of flights as the strike action aggravated attempts by the airport to recover from a five-hour shutdown on Tuesday due to a fire.

The conservative government took office in May after 13 years of Socialist rule. It sparked mass protests in July by announcing a freeze on public sector salaries in 1997 to trim the budget in line with criteria for Europe's planned single currency.

The unions, led by the Workers' Commission (CCOO) and by UGT, say the freeze violates a deal with the previous Socialist administration which guaranteed wages would rise next year in line with inflation.
The deadlock looked set to continue with unions vowing on Wednesday to keep up the fight.

"Today's strike is the beginning of the end and the problem will not be resolved after the strike is over.....the issue needs to be discussed with the government," said UGT representative Julio de la Cuerda.
The government reiterated on Wednesday that the freeze was not negotiable.
